title: Module 10 · Lesson 2 — Communicating uncertainty and designing against automation bias

lines: Module Ten, Lesson Two: communicating uncertainty, and designing against automation bias.
An oversight step that people rubber-stamp provides no oversight at all.
Picture a law firm where an AI assistant reviews contracts, and a paralegal named Sam checks each clause it marks as fine.
For months, the assistant is right, again and again.
So Sam stops reading and just clicks accept.
Then a risky auto-renewal clause gets a confident all-clear, and it slips straight through.
That's automation bias: the tendency to over-trust automated output and stop checking it.
It gets worse as the system gets better, so the fix has to live in the design.
First, show the evidence, not just the conclusion, so review is real rather than performative.
Then surface uncertainty, and make low-confidence clauses look different so they demand attention.
Require an active decision, with no pre-selected accept button, and ask for a brief reason on override.
Rotate and train reviewers on known failure cases, so they stay healthily doubtful.
Then sample-audit the approvals, and measure the override rate.
A rate near zero across thousands of reviews is evidence of rubber-stamping, not perfection.
Next, communicate confidence honestly.
Raw model probabilities are poorly calibrated, so never show them as precise percentages.
Better signals are retrieval scores, whether sources agree, and self-consistency across samples.
Show simple high, medium and low bands, tied to a calibrated threshold.
Language models sound fluent and sure whether they're right or not, so overconfident language is a design defect.
If the assistant can't answer well, it should say so, and point to someone who can help.
Transparency is both a regulatory expectation and good design.
Tell users they're talking to an AI, cite the sources, explain its limits, and show a visible route to a human.
For consequential decisions, add a documented appeal and override path.
A person must be able to contest the outcome, and reach someone with the authority to change it.
Finally, make feedback cheap and specific.
A thumbs-down tells you almost nothing, but quoted an outdated contract version tells you exactly where the pipeline failed.
Capture each correction against its trace ID, and tell the user what changed.
Then route it into the data flywheel, because human corrections are your best training and evaluation data.
On the exam, a near-zero override rate signals rubber-stamping, and options that always produce an answer are wrong.
Honest abstention beats a plausible invention, so read on for the full set of countermeasures.
